item.research_question: How can a strong and ductile medium-entropy alloy be designed to resist hydrogen embrittlement and corrosion?
item.material_system: CoNiV medium-entropy alloy with face-centered cubic structure
item.processing_route: Vacuum induction melting, drop-casting, homogenization at 1200 °C for 24 h, cold-rolling to 75% thickness reduction, and recrystallization annealing at 950 °C for 1 h
item.test_conditions: Slow strain rate tensile testing at 10−4 s−1, hydrogen charging at 50 mA cm−2 in 0.5 M H2SO4 solution, and corrosion testing in 0.1 M H2SO4 solution
key_findings: The CoNiV MEA shows high resistance to hydrogen embrittlement at ambient temperature
The alloy has a low hydrogen diffusivity of ~10−13 m2 s−1
The formation of a dense oxide film on the alloy surface reduces the hydrogen uptake rate and provides high corrosion resistance
The alloy exhibits a good strength-ductility relation combined with high resistance to corrosion
The total elongation drops by only ~1.5% in the presence of hydrogen
The corrosion current density remains below 7 μA cm−2
item.mechanism: The alloy's solid solution hardened single face-centered cubic phase structure, devoid of precipitations, provides low hydrogen diffusivity and absence of local electrochemical potential gradients. The solute hydrogen in the bulk alloy matrix leads to the formation of deformation twins, which impede crack propagation.
quotes: a strong and ductile medium-entropy alloy resists hydrogen embrittlement and corrosion
the material under investigation shows no obvious hydrogen embrittlement at a temperature of 300 K and a strain rate of 10−4 s−1
the alloy forms a stable oxide film with a low concentration of point defects and metal hydroxides which inhibits hydrogen liberation and diffusion as well as corrosion
